alt: Question 1 on Topic 1, Research Methods, is compulsory and covers key questions 1.1 to 1.3. Candidates then choose one more question, on either Topic 2, Identity: Self and Society, or Topic 3, Social Stratification and Inequality.
caption: Research Methods cannot be avoided; then pick Identity or Inequality.

alt: Research Methods sits at the centre, linked to identity, inequality, family, education and crime, because exam questions on any of these can ask candidates to suggest or evaluate a research method for that topic.
caption: Research Methods is never finished: it returns inside questions on every other topic.

after: ## Evaluating a research method — the four-part structure
alt: Four boxes for evaluating a research method: practical issues (time, cost, access), ethical issues (consent, harm, confidentiality), theoretical issues (validity versus reliability) and representativeness of the sample. A note says practical issues alone will not reach the top band.
caption: Cover practical, ethical, theoretical and representativeness points, not just practical ones.

after: ## Identity and inequality — a genuinely connected pair
alt: Two boxes linked by arrows in both directions. A person’s position in the stratification system shapes the identity formed through socialisation, and that identity in turn reinforces the position. A working-class identity is the example.
caption: Link Topics 2 and 3 both ways for a synthesised answer.

after: ## Identity and inequality — a genuinely connected pair
alt: Formal social control works through explicit rules and sanctions enforced by government, the police, the courts and the penal system. Informal social control works through unwritten norms enforced by family, peers and media through disapproval, praise, gossip and exclusion.
caption: Formal control uses written rules and penalties; informal control uses everyday reactions.

after: ## Why sampling matters as much as method choice
alt: A population of mixed coloured dots leads to two samples. A representative sample contains the same mix and allows findings to be generalised with more confidence. A small, unrepresentative or self-selecting sample contains only one colour and undermines even a well-designed method.
caption: A good method with a poor sample still gives weak evidence.
